installation.note: ln is a built-in command available on all Linux systems by default

overview.summary: ln (link) creates links between files. There are two types: hard links (direct reference to file data) and symbolic links (pointers to file paths). Symbolic links are more common and flexible - they can point to directories and work across file systems. Hard links are limited to files on the same file system.
when_to_use: Create hard links for file references

syntax.description: Create link named LINK_NAME pointing to TARGET. Default creates hard link. Use -s for symbolic link.

misconceptions.title: Links are copies
misconceptions.reality: Links are references, not copies. Symbolic links point to file paths, hard links point to file data. No data is duplicated.
misconceptions.tip: Links are references, not copies. Changes to original affect link, and vice versa. No extra disk space used.

misconceptions.title: Hard links and symbolic links are the same
misconceptions.misconception: Hard and symbolic links work identically
misconceptions.reality: Hard links point to file data (same file system only, files only). Symbolic links point to paths (work across file systems, can point to directories).
misconceptions.tip: Use symbolic links (-s) for most cases - more flexible. Hard links are less common and have limitations.

common_pitfalls.solution: Ensure target exists before creating link. Use ls -l to check if link is broken (target missing).

common_pitfalls.description: Trying to create hard link to directory
common_pitfalls.solution: Hard links only work for files. Use symbolic links (-s) for directories.
Use absolute paths for links that need to work from anywhere. Relative paths work but break if directory structure changes.

related_commands.relationship: View links; ls -l shows link information

related_commands.relationship: Link info; readlink shows link target

best_practices: Use symbolic links (-s) for most cases - more flexible
Use absolute paths for links that need to work from anywhere
Verify links with ls -l to see targets
Use symbolic links for directories (hard links don't work)
Check for broken links: ls -l shows broken links clearly
Use -f to overwrite existing links if needed
performance_tips: Links are very fast - just file system metadata
No performance impact - links are just references

additional_notes.symbolic_vs_hard: Symbolic links (-s) = point to path, flexible, can point to directories. Hard links = point to data, same file system only, files only.
additional_notes.most_common: Symbolic links are most common - use ln -s for most cases
additional_notes.verification: Use ls -l to see links - shows 'l' type and -> target. Broken links show red or different color.
additional_notes.common_use: Very common: ln -s target link (create), ln -s /usr/bin/program shortcut (program shortcut), ln -s ../config .config (config link)
